First Love. Ivan Turgenev's First Love captures the emotional turbulence of adolescence through a young man's tender infatuation with a beautiful older woman who has just moved into his neighborhood. The unnamed narrator, a sheltered sixteen-year-old, becomes obsessed with Zinaida, a sophisticated young woman three years his senior who hosts fashionable gatherings. He constructs an idealized vision of her, believing her superior to all others, and experiences the exquisite pain of unrequited desire mixed with fleeting moments of encouragement. Zinaida is surrounded by suitors of various ages and ranks, and the narrator's jealousy and confusion grow as he struggles to understand her behavior and her true feelings toward him. Then comes the shocking discovery that his own father, married and mature, has become romantically entangled with Zinaida. This betrayal shatters the boy's illusions, revealing her moral complexity—she is capable of genuine feeling but also calculation. The novella ends with the narrator older, reflecting on how his first love, though painful, taught him both the intensity of youthful passion and the necessity of disillusionment. Turgenev's prose captures the poignancy of remembering one's own past with both tenderness and ironic distance, making it one of his most autobiographical and emotionally nuanced works.
